authoredPrompt: This figure places two space-filling molecular models side by side on a white ground, labeled "(a)" and "(b)" in small type beneath them. In model (a), two large green spheres each labeled "Cl" sit at the upper left and upper right, and a single red sphere labeled "O" is wedged between them and forward, sitting lower, so the three atoms describe a shallow V with the oxygen at the vertex. The spheres carry soft highlights and interpenetrate where the atoms are bonded, giving the fused outline of a space-filling representation rather than balls joined by sticks. Model (b) reverses the pattern: one large green sphere labeled "Cl" occupies the lower center and two red spheres labeled "O" rise from it at the upper left and upper right, again bent, this time with chlorine at the vertex. The red oxygens are noticeably smaller than the green chlorines, reflecting relative atomic size. Drawing both at one scale in one style asks the reader to compare which atom sits at the center and how many of each kind surround it. The pair are dichlorine monoxide and chlorine dioxide, the chlorine oxides used commercially for bleaching pulp and flour and for treating water.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between Cl2O and ClO2 focus views: one molecule enlarges while the other dims, and the central atom plus surrounding atoms are labeled, making clear how changing the formula changes which element sits at the vertex.
- Click the central atom in either model to highlight the two attached atoms, making clear the connection between atom size, atom count, and the V-shaped molecular arrangement.
authoredContext:
As a class, the oxides are extremely reactive and unstable, and their chemistry has little practical importance. Dichlorine oxide, formally called dichlorine monoxide, and chlorine dioxide, both shown in the figure, are the only commercially important compounds. They are important as bleaching agents (for use with pulp and flour) and for water treatment.

This image shows the structures of the (a) Cl2O and (b) ClO2 molecules.

Two space filling models are shown and labeled, “a,” and “b.” Model a shows a red atom labeled, “O,” bonded to two green atoms labeled, “C l,” in a v-shape. Model b shows a green atom labeled, “C l,” bonded to two red atoms labeled, “O,” in a v-shape.
